newsitem.title: USA: Quaker posts $1.11 billion loss; chairman may leave.
newsitem.headline: Quaker posts $1.11 billion loss; chairman may leave.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co., as expected, Wednesday posted a staggering quarterly loss of $1.1 billion for the sale of its Snapple beverage business, and said it was seeking a replacement for Chairman William D. Smithburg.

Smithburg, who plans to step down after 16 years at the helm of Quaker, is blamed for the decision to pay $1.7 billion for Snapple in December 1994, and for holding on to the business despite its drain on the company's profits.
Quaker said it formed a committee to find a replacement for Smithburg, 58, who will continue to run the company in the meantime. He also holds the post of chief executive.
Quaker took a one-time charge of $1.14 billion for the pending sale of Snapple to Triarch Cos for $300 million. It disclosed the charge when it announced the sale last month.
The $1.11 billion loss for the quarter, which equalled $8.15 a share, compared with net income of $32.2 million a year earlier.
Excluding the one-time charge, Quaker said it earned 24 cents a share, which was up from 22 cents a year earlier and better than market analysts had expected.
Sales declined to $1.20 billion from $1.22 billion.
Quaker also said it might sell non-core businesses as part of a plan to reduce costs, repurchase shares and focus on its core businesses. It did not identify the units.
"The results of our core businesses were strong," Smithburg said in a statement. "We're pleased with 9 percent earnings growth from ongoing businesses ..."
Quaker said ready-to-eat cereal volume grew 27 percent, which outpaced the rest of the industry.
"At the same time, U.S. Gatorade reported 15 percent volume growth, and our U.S. hot cereals grew 4 percent," Smithburg said.

Worldwide foods operating income fell to $78.0 million in the quarter from $99.9 million, excluding divested businesses and a gain. The decline was due to an average 15 percent price cut on U.S. ready-to-eat cereals and greater advertising and merchandising spending.
Operating income at Quaker's U.S. and Canadian foods unit fell 22 percent to $77.2 million from $99.0 million a year ago. Sales edged up to $665.3 million from $651.6 million.

Hot and ready-to-eat cerals, Golden Grain, Aunt Jemima, regional grain products and Canadian foods all had good sales gains, Quaker said. These were offset by volume and income declines in grain-based snacks and in food service.
Overall volume was up 3 percent for U.S. and Canadian foods.
International food sales rose 3 percent to $155.2 million from $150.3 million, excluding the Italian products businesses sold in 1996. Operating income slid to $800,000 from $900,000.

While Snapple has been a dismal failure, worldwide sales of Quaker's Gatorade sports drinks shot up 13 percent to $284.6 million from $251.8 million. Worldwide Gatorade operating income soared 231 percent to $34.4 million.
International Gatorade sales of $71.0 million rose 7 percent to $66.1 million, due largely to growth in Latin America, it said.
Quaker's stock gained 50 cents to $38.75 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
